description: We are a 3 person team with complementary backgrounds in geospatial technologies, AI, and data science. One member studies Applied Geomatics ingeneering at UNSTIM, while the other two are pursuing training in Digitalisation and Data Science at SCITI . United by our experience in NOAI, we are participating in NASA Space Apps 2026 with FireWatch Africa, a geospatial tool that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations to analyze fire activity and historical patterns, starting with Benin.
summary:
FireWatch Benin is an interactive satellite-based fire monitoring and historical analysis platform focused on Benin. It combines NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations to help users explore where and when fire activity occurs, identify seasonal patterns, and compare current activity with historical levels.

The application provides an interactive map, monthly and weekly fire calendars, seasonal trends, anomaly analysis, and downloadable datasets. A key feature is its harmonization method, which addresses inconsistencies between satellite sensors and changes in the number of active VIIRS satellites. For the period before VIIRS observations began in 2012, a machine-learning model estimates comparable VIIRS-equivalent hotspot values from MODIS observations.

By making long-term satellite fire data easier to explore and compare, FireWatch Benin aims to support evidence-based understanding of fire activity and provide an accessible starting point for further environmental monitoring and research.
details:
How it works

FireWatch Benin processes historical NASA satellite active-fire detections and transforms them into an interactive monitoring and analysis interface.

Users can explore the whole country or define a custom area using a point and radius, a rectangle, or a drawn polygon. They can then inspect fire activity through monthly and weekly calendars, seasonal comparisons, anomaly views, interactive maps, and long-term trends. The application also allows users to download processed time series, calendar data, detections, and GeoJSON files.

Data harmonization and methodology

A major technical challenge is that MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and observation characteristics. In addition, the number of operational VIIRS satellites changes over time. Directly comparing their raw detection counts can therefore introduce artificial discontinuities.

To address this, FireWatch constructs a common comparison measure called VIIRS-equivalent hotspots. Daily VIIRS detections are normalized by the number of active VIIRS satellites. For the pre-2012 period, when VIIRS observations are unavailable, a gradient-boosting model trained on the 2012–2021 overlap period estimates comparable values from MODIS observations.

The harmonization approach was evaluated using leave-one-year-out validation. The model achieved an R² of 0.92 for cell-level monthly estimates and 0.989 for monthly national totals. These are validation results, not a guarantee that every individual hotspot corresponds to a confirmed ground fire.

Findings from the current analysis

The current analysis indicates that December and January account for approximately 61% of detections in a typical year. The estimated long-term trend since 2002 is a decline of approximately 4.5% per year. Fire activity from 1–15 November 2026 is approximately 28% below the median for the same dates across 2001–2025.

These findings describe satellite-derived hotspot detections and should be interpreted with the limitations of satellite observation in mind.

Tools and intended impact

The project was developed using Python and Streamlit, with data processing, machine learning, geospatial analysis, and interactive visualization tools.

FireWatch Benin is designed to make long-term satellite fire information more accessible to researchers, students, local organizations, and people interested in environmental monitoring. Its main contribution is not simply displaying fire detections, but making historical comparisons more meaningful through an explicit harmonization process.

Limitations

Satellite hotspots are indicators of thermal anomalies, not confirmed records of individual ground fires. Cloud cover and sensor characteristics can affect detection. The geographic boundary currently used for the country outline is also a limitation of the map.

Super Intelligence disclosure

ChatGPT and Claude were used as AI-assisted development tools for technical guidance, coding support, debugging, and preparation of project documentation. NASA satellite observations remain the underlying source of the fire data; the harmonization and analysis results are produced by the project's processing workflow.
